sketch: Two players defending one carrier, forechecking towards the net on the right: the first pressures, and the second layers diagonally behind them, two or three stick lengths back, rather than converging on the same puck, where one pass beats you both. First and second are the order they arrive in, not two particular players. A deliberate double-team — commonly allowed below your own goal line, where a turnover is contained by the net and the boards — is a coaching decision rather than something to freelance, so ask your coach where and when your team doubles. Whether the first player’s arrival may end in a hit depends on whether your game allows body checking. ⚠️ Arrive on the carrier’s inside, stick on the ice inside them, and never into the back of a player facing the boards.

sketch: The wedge+1 penalty kill, 4-on-5, against a power-play 1-3-1 with the puck on the half-wall. Three killers hold a tight triangle around the net and do not chase: two defencemen just off the crease edges, drawn wider apart than they really stand, and one forward at the mid-to-high slot. All three are marked W, for wedge rather than winger. The +1 hurries whoever has the puck, stick on the puck, here straight out from the goal toward the carrier: one of three published routes, and a coaching choice. Whether that pressure may end in a hit depends on whether your game allows body checking. Be in the lane before the shot, not sliding into it, and never block from a screening position. ⚠️ Block from close and on your feet, head out of the lane, hands behind your body with the backs of the gloves out.

sketch: One instant, everything visible before the pass: the puck is coming to you on the half-wall and a forechecker is closing. No look is drawn: the notation has no head. Pressure could come from the middle too, so check both shoulders. The retriever could be any teammate. Looking does not protect you; position does. Whether the forechecker may hit you depends on whether your game allows body checking. A reception on the wall can end with you against the boards, checking league or not. Get your skates parallel to the wall and take any contact on your forearm and hip, head up and chin off your chest — not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it. If you are already facing the wall and cannot turn, get your stick and gloves up and spread out on the glass, with no head contact at all. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck.

sketch: Going back for a puck in your own corner with a checker inside your line; only your line is drawn. It arrives on an angle and finishes running along the boards: the first and best of three cases. The second case: get your skates parallel to the wall and take it on your forearm and hip. The worst, for when you already face the wall, is damage limitation rather than a position to aim for. Turn your skates parallel first if at all possible; failing that, spread the load, with stick and gloves up on the glass, arms out as a shock absorber, and no head contact at all. The cases come from USA Hockey's material; the ordering and ranking do not. ⚠️ Never turn your back to anyone coming at you, and never duck.

sketch: Rimming past a checker who has sealed you against the boards, in your own end. Keep the puck on the far side of your body from them, as drawn, and keep your feet wide and low and still moving: a stationary player on the wall gets pinned. Decide where the puck is going while you are still skating to it. Skates parallel to the boards, forearm and hip to the wall, head up and chin off your chest — and not on the point of your shoulder, and not the whole shoulder if you can help it. ⚠️ Rim or reverse, never turn your back to anyone coming at you and never duck. Those are two different injuries — a hit from behind you cannot brace for, and a chin tucked to the chest, which does not need speed to do it.
